unit.title: Budgeting and saving
unit.description: Know where your money goes, build your emergency fund and free up money to invest every month

texts: Where has my pay gone?
Laura
Almost at zero at the end of the month again. But I earn €1,400!
I don't even know what I spend it on.
What would you advise her to do first?
Stop going out and not buy anything else
Cutting back blindly rarely lasts. First you need to know **where** the money goes.
Look at her bank transactions for the last month
That's it! It's the real picture of her spending, not the one she imagines. With that she can make her **budget**.
Ask for an advance on her salary
An advance just pushes the problem on to next month… and sometimes with fees.
Laura opens her banking app and starts writing things down…
Fixed or variable
These are Laura's expenses from last month. Split them up: **fixed** ones are almost the same every month; **variable** ones change and depend more on her.
Fixed
Variable
Rent
It's the same every month: the only way to cut it is to move or share.
Food delivery
It changes every month and depends on her: variable.
Phone plan
The same amount every month. You cut it once, by switching plans.
Clothes
Variable: some months a lot, others nothing.
Monthly travel pass
Fixed: she pays the same every month.
Going out and leisure
Variable, and it's usually where there's most room to cut.
Groceries
It changes every month depending on what she buys: variable.
Two streaming services
They're charged automatically every month: fixed (and easy to forget).
Sort all her expenses.
Laura spends **€1,372**: €512 fixed and €860 variable. Out of her €1,400 she has €28 left. That's the problem… and also where the room is: fixed costs are cut once; variable ones, every day.
Hint: does she pay the same every month? Then it's fixed.
Fixed or variable? Choose for each expense

steps.title: What you have left is what you can invest
steps.body:
Income − spending = what you have left each month. That figure fills your emergency fund first and then your **regular contributions**: even if it's €50 a month, compound interest starts working.

If nothing is left, your budget tells you where to find it: almost always, in your variable spending.
steps.key: If you don't know where your money goes, you can't decide where it goes.
steps.tip: Try it: buy an ETF in the simulator with what you have left each month.

texts: Split Laura's pay
Laura takes home **€1,400** and wants to start investing. The **50/30/20** rule says: 50 % for needs, 30 % for wants and 20 % for saving. This is what her spending looks like now:
Needs
Wants
Savings
Rent
Groceries
Monthly travel pass
Phone plan
Going out and leisure
Food delivery
Clothes
Two streaming services
With this spending, how much can Laura save each month?
About €30
About €150
The same spending as in the previous lesson: needs, €760; wants, €612. She's left with **€28**. It's not that she earns too little: it all goes on day-to-day stuff.
Adjust the spending so Laura saves at least 20 %.
With saving **set aside first**, the rest sorts itself out. That 20 % is what fills your emergency fund and, after that, your contributions to invest.
Careful! This way she spends more than she earns.
Nearly! One more little push and she hits 20 %.
Wants are already where they should be. Can she save something on groceries or rent?
Start with what has the most room: wants

steps.title: When it doesn't add up
steps.body: The rule was popularised by US senator Elizabeth Warren. In expensive cities, rent alone can take 40 % of your pay. Then you adjust, but **always with a percentage set aside for savings**, even if it starts at 5 %.
steps.key: The exact numbers aren't what matters: what matters is that saving has its own fixed share.
steps.tip: Try it: ask your tutor Lumi how you'd split your salary with 50/30/20.

texts: Hunt down your small leaks
A **small leak** is a small, frequent expense. One on its own goes unnoticed… but all of them together? Switch off the ones you could drop without missing them.
Takeaway coffee
Vending-machine fizzy drink
Delivery fees
Third streaming service
Gym you never go to
In-game top-ups
A €1.80 takeaway coffee every day. How much is that in a year?
About €65
About €650
About €1,800
€1.80 × 365 days = **€657** a year. Small things, repeated, add up to big ones.
Cut at least €1,000 a year without dropping everything.
It's not about never spending, but about spending on what **really** matters to you. What you cut, invested for years, grows with compound interest (7 % is an example, not a promise).
All gone! No need to be that strict: keep what you really enjoy.
Every switch you flip off is money for you Check the number below.
Switch off what you could drop without missing it

steps.title: Subscriptions
steps.body:
Streaming, music, gym, apps, cloud storage… They charge you automatically, which is why you forget them. Four subscriptions at €12 are €48 a month: **€576 a year**.

Check your statement and ask yourself about each one: have I used it this month? Lots of free trials turn into paid plans if you don't cancel them.
steps.key: Small, repeated costs add up: check your charges once a month.
steps.tip: Try it: buy an ETF in the simulator with what you cut this month.

texts: A year full of surprises

Laura earns €1,400 and, after adjusting her budget, spends €1,200 a month. Things are going to happen to her this year, like they do to everyone. Decide how much she puts aside each month and live the year.
Her phone breaks
Emergency trip to the dentist
The car breaks down
If Laura puts nothing aside, what happens when the surprises arrive?
Nothing: she'll manage somehow
She pays with her card and ends up owing money with interest
The bank pays for them for free
Without a cushion, every surprise turns into **debt**, and card debt charges high interest.
Live the year without ending up owing anything on the card.
That cushion is your **emergency fund**: money set aside only for the unexpected. The usual rule: between **3 and 6 months of expenses** (6 to 12 if your job is unstable).
Ouch! The surprise went on the card… and now it's charging interest. Try putting more aside.
Now hit «Live the year» and see what happens.
Choose how much Laura puts aside each month and hit «Live the year»
March 2020
Leo
March 2020. Leo has €4,000 in an S&P 500 ETF and no emergency fund.
The stock market is crashing because of the virus and I've been furloughed.
I need €1,000 this month and the only place I have it is the ETF…
What would have saved him?
Having a separate emergency fund
That's it: he pays from the fund and the ETF can wait to recover.
Having sold everything just before the fall
Nobody knows when a fall is coming. An emergency fund works without guessing.
Taking out a payday loan so as not to touch the ETF
He doesn't sell at a loss, but pays sky-high interest. The fund costs nothing.
Without a fund, you're forced to **sell at the worst moment**. With one, you decide.

steps.title: Where to keep it
steps.body:
It has to be **available and risk-free**: an interest-paying account, a deposit you can cancel without losing what you put in, or Treasury bills (Letras del Tesoro) for part of it.

Deposits are covered by the **Fondo de Garantía de Depósitos (Spain's deposit guarantee scheme) up to €100,000** per holder per bank. **Not in the stock market:** crises bring layoffs and market falls at the same time.
steps.key: A half-built cushion already saves you from plenty of scares: start with one month of expenses.
steps.tip: Try it: set a price alert 20 % below your ETF's price.

texts: Pablo's experiment
Pablo
This month I'm going to save **whatever's left** at the end of the month. There's bound to be something!
Day 30…
Well… €12 left over. I don't know how, but it always all goes
What do you suggest for next month?
Try again with more willpower
Willpower runs out. Spending stretches to fill your pay: there's almost never anything «left over».
Set up a €150 transfer for payday
That's **paying yourself first**! The savings go out on their own on payday and you spend what's left.
Keep his loose change in a piggy bank
Better than nothing, but coins won't get him far. A fixed, automatic percentage works better.
A month later…
I put aside €150 and didn't even notice! I spent a bit less without realising.
What a habit can do
What if Pablo keeps that automatic transfer going for years and invests it? Let's say 5 % a year: it's an example, not a promise.
Reach €100,000 putting aside €200 a month at most.
Automatic saving doesn't depend on your willpower. Start with 5-10 % of your pay and raise it with every pay rise: time does the rest.
That's easy… but the challenge is to do it with €200 a month at most!
Notice how much time adds compared with what you put in.
Move the years and how much he puts aside each month

steps.title: Automate it
steps.body:
1. Open a separate account for your savings.
2. Set up a **standing order** for the day after payday.
3. Once your emergency fund is full, turn that transfer into a **regular contribution** to your ETF.
4. Start with a percentage that doesn't hurt (5-10 %) and raise it with every pay rise.
steps.key: Save first; then spend what's left.
steps.tip: Try it: pick in Market the ETF your transfer will go to and add it to Favourites.

u2l1-1.prompt: Match each concept with an example.
u2l1-1.explanation: Income − spending (fixed and variable) = savings. It's the basic sum behind any budget.
right: What's left at the end of the month

u2l1-3.prompt: What's the best way to start a budget?
options: Work out from memory what you think you spend
Wait until you earn more to start
u2l1-3.explanation: Memory plays tricks: nearly all of us think we spend less than we do. Your bank statement is the real picture.

u2l1-6.prompt: Ana earns €1,200 a month and her fixed costs are already €660 (55 %). Split 100 % of her pay: cover the fixed costs, keep at least 10 % for savings and don't go over 35 % on variable costs.
u2l1-6.explanation: With 55 % fixed and at least 10 % saved, variable costs get 35 % at most: groceries and going out share that gap.

u2l1-10.prompt: What counts as income? Tick all.
options: What you're paid for private tutoring
u2l1-10.explanation: Income is what comes in and is yours: your salary, what you're paid for tutoring. Rent is an expense, and a loan has to be paid back: it isn't income.

u2l1-11.prompt: Laura finds she spends €160 a month on takeaway food and cuts it in half. She doesn't have an emergency fund yet. What does she do with the €80 she frees up?
options: She leaves it in her current account, with no plan
She sets it aside: first the cushion, then investing
She spends it on clothes: she's already cut back, after all
u2l1-11.explanation: A cut only works if that money has somewhere to go: first the emergency fund, then investing. Leaving it in the account seems just as good, but without a plan it ends up spent.
feedback: Money with nowhere to go ends up spent without you noticing.
Once the fund is full, that €80 becomes her monthly contribution to an ETF.
The cut vanishes and she's back at zero by the end of the month.

u2l1-12.prompt: Lumi wants to start investing, but doesn't know how much she can afford or where to begin. What do you reply?
options: Invest everything you have in your account: the sooner the better
Wait until you earn more to start
Look at your transactions and work out what's left
u2l1-12.explanation: What you can invest comes from your real budget, not a guess. Investing everything is tempting, but without an emergency fund any scare forces you to sell.
feedback: Without an emergency fund, the first surprise forces you to sell, maybe at a loss.
With a bigger salary, spending usually goes up too: starting early and small counts for more.
That's it! You'll know how much you can put in each month without overdoing it.
lines: I want to start investing, but I don't know how much I can afford.

u2l2-4.prompt: Split a €1,500 salary with the 50/30/20 rule: at most 50 % on needs and 30 % on wants, and at least 20 % saved.
u2l2-4.explanation: With €1,500: up to €750 on needs, up to €450 on wants and at least €300 saved.

u2l2-6.prompt: If rent already takes 45 % of your pay, the best thing is to stop saving until that changes.
u2l2-6.explanation: Better to adjust the percentages (for example, by cutting wants) and keep saving something, even if it's a little.

u2l2-7.prompt: In the 50/30/20 rule, ____ % goes to savings and paying off debt.

u2l2-9.prompt: Laura takes home €1,800 and her needs already add up to €1,000 (56 %). What does she do?
options: Trims her wants a little and keeps saving
Stops saving until she gets a pay rise
Pays for her wants on her credit card in instalments
u2l2-9.explanation: The rule adapts: if needs weigh more, you cut wants, not savings.
feedback: She has €440 left for wants (24 %): she adapts the rule to her rent without giving up saving.
That could take a long time, and with no cushion any surprise ends up as debt.
That way the 30 % turns into debt with interest: the hole grows every month.

u2l2-11.prompt: Your emergency fund is full and you have no expensive debt. What do you do with your 20 % each month?
options: Keep growing the emergency fund with no limit
Buy each month the share that rose most the week before
An automatic contribution to a global index ETF
u2l2-11.explanation: Once the fund is full, the 20 % becomes your contribution to invest for the long term. Buying whatever has risen most is tempting, but that's letting FOMO drive.
feedback: Safe, but money you won't need for years loses purchasing power.
That's chasing trends: you buy expensive what has already gone up.
Your savings start working every month without you having to decide anything.

u2l2-12.prompt: What goes in the rule's 20 % for saving? Mark all that apply.
options: Paying off an expensive debt early
u2l2-12.explanation: The 20 % is for your future self: emergency fund, getting rid of expensive debt and investing. Rent goes in the 50 % for needs and the gym in the 30 % for wants.

u2l3-4.prompt: Which are typical small leaks? Tick all.
u2l3-4.explanation: Small leaks are small, frequent and almost invisible: coffee, micro-purchases, delivery fees. Rent or a mortgage are big fixed costs.

u2l3-6.prompt: Marta checks her statement and finds five subscriptions: she uses two every week and hasn't opened three in months. What does she do?
options: Cancels them all, including the ones she uses every day
Cancels the ones she doesn't use and keeps the others
Leaves everything: it's not much money
u2l3-6.explanation: The goal is to spend on what you value, not to punish yourself.
feedback: Cutting what you enjoy usually ends in a relapse: better to cut what you don't use.
She gets that money back every month without giving up what she does enjoy.
Not much a month, but over a year it could pay for a weekend away.

u2l3-7.prompt: Put the steps for clearing out your subscriptions in order.
options: Make a list of all recurring payments
Mark the ones you didn't use last month
Go through your statement for the last 3 months
u2l3-7.explanation: First look, then decide and, finally, send what you recover to savings before it gets spent on something else.

u2l3-8.prompt: Many free trials automatically become paid if you don't cancel them.
u2l3-8.explanation: That's why it's worth noting the date the trial ends.

u2l3-11.prompt: You cut €60 a month on subscriptions you weren't using. You already have an emergency fund. What do you do so the money doesn't just vanish?
options: I give it a purpose that same day
I treat myself to something for €60 to celebrate
I leave it in my current account, I'll see
u2l3-11.explanation: A cut only counts if that money has an automatic destination. Leaving it in the account seems enough, but what isn't set aside gets spent.
feedback: The money changes destination before you miss it, and starts to grow.
Once is fine, but if it keeps happening, the cut was for nothing.
With nowhere to go, it drains away on other small spending.

u2l3-12.prompt: Lumi spends €3 a day at the uni vending machine and asks whether investing it would change anything. What do you reply?
options: Only if you invest it in crypto, which is what rises most
Yes: small and repeated ends up adding up to a lot
u2l3-12.explanation: A small expense repeated every day adds up to a lot over a year, and if it's invested, compound interest makes it bigger. Thinking «it's only €3» is tempting, but what weighs is how often.
feedback: What matters is consistency and time, not chasing whatever rises most.
That's more than €1,000 a year; invested for years, quite a bit more.
That's it! And you don't have to cut it all: even half shows.
lines: I spend €3 a day at the vending machine at uni.
If I invested it, would it change anything?

u2l4-2.prompt: What is the emergency fund based on?
u2l4-2.explanation: What you need to cover in an emergency is your expenses, not your salary.

u2l4-3.prompt: Is it suitable for holding your emergency fund?
options: A deposit you can cancel without losing capital
u2l4-3.explanation: The cushion has to be available and not at risk of falling right when you need it.

u2l4-4.prompt: Pablo has a €3,000 cushion and the car he uses for work breaks down: €800 to fix. What does he do?
options: Pays with the cushion and tops it up bit by bit
Pays on his credit card in instalments so as not to touch the cushion
Sells his investments even though they're at a loss
u2l4-4.explanation: A surprise paid from the cushion costs no interest and doesn't force you to sell at a bad moment.
feedback: That's what it's for: no debt or interest, and in a few months it's full again.
He pays interest while the money sits idle right next to him: this is what the cushion is for.
He had money available and still turned a temporary dip into a real loss.

u2l4-8.prompt: Which are real emergencies? Tick all.
options: A breakdown of the car you use for work
u2l4-8.explanation: An emergency is unexpected and necessary: a breakdown of the car you work with, losing your job, an unexpected medical bill. The sales and holidays can be planned for.

u2l4-9.prompt: Bruno has €10,000, no debt and spends €1,000 a month. How does he organise it?
options: All in the stock market, it earns more than sitting idle
€6,000 as a cushion and €4,000 for the long term
All in his current account at 0 %
u2l4-9.explanation: First the cushion, then invest what you won't need for years.
feedback: If something unexpected happens in the middle of a fall, he'll have to sell at a loss.
He has 6 months covered and the rest can ride out falls without stress.
Safe, but the €4,000 he won't need for years loses purchasing power.

u2l4-10.prompt: The usual cushion is between 3 and ____ months of expenses.
u2l4-10.explanation: 3 to 6 months of expenses; more if your income is unstable.

u2l4-11.prompt: Your ETF portfolio falls 25 % and, the same week, you get a €900 repair bill. You have a 3-month emergency fund. What do you do?
options: Sell part of the ETF to pay for it
Pay it from the emergency fund
Pay it on the card in instalments
u2l4-11.explanation: The emergency fund exists so you never have to sell your investments in the middle of a fall. Selling a little seems prudent, but it locks in the loss at exactly the worst moment.
feedback: You turn a temporary fall into a real loss with the money right there.
The fall stays temporary as long as you don't sell, and the fund has done its job.
You pay interest while sitting on a fund meant for exactly this.

u2l5-1.prompt: Put in order the month of someone who pays themselves first.
options: The automatic transfer to savings goes out
Spends what's left on variable costs
u2l5-1.explanation: Savings go out before any spending: that way they don't compete with treats.

u2l5-4.prompt: Match each trick with why it works.
options: Raising the % with every pay rise
Doing it the day after payday
u2l5-4.explanation: Separate, automate and increase bit by bit: the system works for you.
right: It doesn't depend on your willpower
You pay yourself before anyone else
Savings grow without you feeling the cut
You don't spend your savings without noticing

u2l5-5.prompt: Pablo gets a €200 a month pay rise. What does he do?
options: Spends it all: he'll save when he earns more
Raises his automatic saving by €100 and enjoys the rest
Buys a better car with a payment of €200 a month, every month
u2l5-5.explanation: Putting part of every pay rise into savings is the most painless way to save more.
feedback: Spending rises to match the salary and savings stay the same as before.
He improves his life and his savings at the same time, without feeling any cut.
The whole rise goes on a monthly payment for years.

u2l5-8.prompt: What works is saving ____ spending, not what's left over.
u2l5-8.explanation: Pay yourself first: savings go out when you get paid.

u2l5-9.prompt: Marta earns €2,000 and wants to save €300 a month. When does she schedule the transfer?
options: On the 30th, if there's anything left
u2l5-9.explanation: Right after getting paid, before the money gets mixed up with spending.

u2l5-11.prompt: Pablo's emergency fund is now full, and his €150 transfer still goes out every month. What does he do with it now?
options: He switches it to long-term investing
He stops it and spends the €150
He keeps growing the emergency fund forever
u2l5-11.explanation: Paying yourself first works to fill the emergency fund and, after that, to invest without thinking about it. Growing the fund forever seems prudent, but that idle money loses against inflation.
feedback: The habit is already built: now his money also works for him.
He loses the habit that was hardest for him to build.
A huge emergency fund earns nothing: money he won't need for years loses purchasing power.
